claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by configurational entropy and atomic-size mismatch.
Configurational entropy and atomic-size mismatch favor formation and retention of a single-phase FCC or BCC solid solution over intermetallic phases.
A homogeneous solid solution without brittle intermetallics enables retention of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
The initial alloy is equiatomic or near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni in an as-cast or homogenized state.
Al content will be varied from 0 to 20 at% while the other elements are kept constant.
The controlled heat treatment is annealing at 1000°C for 24 hours followed by cooling to room temperature.
The relevant structural mediator is whether the alloy is a single-phase FCC/BCC solid solution or a multiphase microstructure containing intermetallics.
High configurational entropy and atomic-size mismatch suppress chemical ordering and intermetallic formation.
Solid-solution microstructural stability prevents embrittlement and preserves mechanical and environmental properties under extreme conditions.
Increasing Al beyond a critical threshold will cause a transition from a stable single-phase solid solution to a multiphase microstructure containing intermetallics.
The Al-induced multiphase transition will decrease toughness, radiation tolerance, and environmental resistance, particularly at cryogenic and high temperatures.
The equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni baseline is a single-phase solid solution with an optimal combination of properties.
The hypothesis is limited to near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni compositions treated below the melting point.
The hypothesis excludes highly non-equiatomic compositions, rapid solidification, and severe plastic deformation.
The precise Al threshold for the proposed phase transition and property degradation is unknown.
Minor elements and processing history may influence the proposed behavior.

contradictions.description: An equiatomic five-component baseline already contains 20 at% Al, while the intervention describes increasing Al only from 0 to 20 at% and predicts degradation upon increasing Al beyond a critical threshold. The comparison direction relative to the stated equiatomic baseline is therefore inconsistent or undefined.

Varying Al from 0 to 20 at% while keeping all other elemental atomic percentages constant is compositionally impossible unless the meaning of 'constant' is changed to fixed ratios or fixed absolute amounts, because atomic percentages must sum to 100.
The hypothesis is bounded to near-equiatomic alloys, but test compositions with 0 or 5 at% Al are substantially non-equiatomic and therefore fall outside the stated boundary.
